China’s 2021 Power Crisis Casts Long Shadow Over Industrial Recovery

China’s sweeping power shortages in late 2021, triggered by an escalating trade dispute and resulting sanctions, left a lasting mark on the nation’s industrial sector. Southwest Aluminum Group Co Ltd is among the firms still reckoning with the aftermath, as analysts assess the broader economic impact of the crisis.

The power crisis began in September 2021, after a series of tit-for-tat sanctions between Beijing and several Western governments escalated in response to political tensions in the South China Sea. Restrictions on coal imports, coupled with diplomatic fallout, led to widespread electricity rationing across key manufacturing hubs. Factories in Chongqing, Guangdong, and Jiangsu provinces were forced to operate on reduced hours, halting production lines and impacting global supply chains.

“Production dropped by 25% in the fourth quarter of 2021,” said Chen Ming, spokesperson for Southwest Aluminum Group Co Ltd. “It was a period of immense uncertainty for our workforce and the entire regional economy.”

According to data from the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association, aluminum output nationwide fell by 14% during the height of the crisis. The China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing reported a contraction in the manufacturing PMI to 49.6 in October 2021, the lowest level in over two years.

While electricity supplies have since stabilized and all major plants have resumed full operations, companies are still navigating the aftereffects. “Supply chain disruptions led to longer lead times for customers and increased costs,” said Zhang Wei, an analyst at Wutai Capital. “The sector is recovering, but the crisis exposed vulnerabilities in China’s energy and trade policies.”

Officials in Chongqing have pledged to diversify energy sources and strengthen contingency planning, vowing that “such widespread disruptions must never be repeated.” Markets are watching closely as the industry adapts to a new geopolitical landscape.
